Sakhawat: Govt to launch door-to-door health screening program
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Wednesday said the government will launch a nationwide home-to-home health screening program to detect diseases at an early stage among the general population.
"Every citizen has the right to receive healthcare services, and no one will be deprived of healthcare. To ensure better public health and facilitate the early detection of serious diseases, the government will introduce the home-to-home health screening initiative across the country," he said.
Sakhawat was speaking as the chief guest at the inauguration ceremony of Hygiene for Health Bangladesh at Gulshan Lake Park here.
He said the government plans to recruit 100,000 health workers, 80% of whom will be women. These female health workers will visit households to teach women how to conduct breast and cervical cancer self-examinations so that diseases can be detected at an early stage and treated promptly, he added.
The minister said health workers will carry a special medical kit while visiting homes. They will provide services such as measuring blood pressure, checking body weight, screening for diabetes, conducting lipid profile tests, and performing various other basic health examinations at people's homes, he added.
The minister said maintaining a clean and hygienic environment is essential for staying healthy. He emphasized that public awareness and good health are prerequisites for building a healthy, knowledge-based, and prosperous nation.
Referring to the increasing number of cesarean section deliveries across the country, he said most babies are now being born through cesarean sections. He expressed concern that many newborns are not being given colostrum-the first breast milk, which is the richest natural source of nutrients and antibodies provided by nature.
He attributed the decline in breastfeeding to mothers' busy lifestyles, negligence, and changing living patterns, warning that this trend is pushing many children toward severe malnutrition.
Miss World Bangladesh 2026 title winner Samanzar Sayeed, Gulshan Society president Omar Sadat, National Director of Miss World Bangladesh Azra Mahmood, Executive Director of Manusher Jonno Foundation Shaheen Anam, and General Secretary of the Gulshan Society Mujibur Rahman Mridha were present, among others.

item.title: Experts call for stronger defences against subthreshold threats
item.description:
Security experts have urged Bangladesh to strengthen its national security framework by developing stronger defences against subthreshold threats, as modern conflicts increasingly move beyond traditional battlefields. The remarks were made at a roundtable titled ‘Sub-threshold Conflict: War by Other Means,’ organised by the Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies (BIPSS) in Dhaka on Tuesday.
The event brought together academics, diplomats, former ambassadors, military officials, law enforcement representatives, researchers, and civil society members to discuss emerging security challenges. Dr Niloy Ranjan Biswas, Professor of International Relations at the University of Dhaka, explained that states are increasingly using cyberattacks, disinformation, economic pressure, proxy groups, and hybrid tactics to achieve strategic goals without engaging in open warfare.
BIPSS President Major General A N M Muniruzzaman (Retd) highlighted that the boundary between war and peace is becoming unclear. He called for a whole-of-society approach involving military, economic, technological, and social sectors to improve national resilience.
Experts stressed the need to protect critical infrastructure, enhance cybersecurity, promote media literacy, and strengthen regional cooperation. They also highlighted Bangladesh’s strategic location and growing digital and maritime systems as areas requiring greater attention. The discussion concluded with calls for stronger coordination among policymakers, security agencies, researchers, and citizens to address evolving threats.

item.title: Information Minister: Bangladeshi nationalism reflects inclusive national identity
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon on Wednesday said Bangladeshi nationalism represents an inclusive national identity that embraces all languages, religions, cultures, ethnic groups and communities living in the country.
Speaking as the chief guest at a seminar titled ‘Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and Bangladeshi Nationalism’ at Jagannath University, he said the philosophy recognises every citizen within Bangladesh’s geographical boundaries as an equal and valued part of the national identity.
The seminar was organised by the Jagannath University chapter of the University Teachers’ Association of Bangladesh (UTAB).
Swapon said Pakistan’s creation on the basis of religion proved that religion alone could not sustain unity in a diverse society. He referred to the 1952 Language Movement and the 1971 Liberation War as examples of the challenges faced by a state attempting to unite people through a single identity.
Highlighting the role of former president Ziaur Rahman during the Liberation War, the minister said his leadership and declaration of independence contributed significantly to organising resistance during the early stages of the war.
He said post-independence debates over national identity showed that a language-based identity alone was not equally acceptable to all sections of society. In this context, he said, Ziaur Rahman introduced the concept of citizen-based Bangladeshi nationalism aimed at bringing all citizens together with equal dignity and rights.
Swapon said modern nationalism is shaped not only by language, religion or ethnicity but also by shared interests, territory, constitutional values and aspirations for a common future.
He added that Bangladeshi nationalism respects the country’s diverse identities and remains relevant as a foundation for national unity and solidarity.
Dhaka-7 MP Hamidur Rahman Hamid attended the programme as the special guest, while Jagannath University Vice-Chancellor Prof Md Rais Uddin delivered the keynote address.

item.title: Auction delays leave 9,278 containers stranded at Ctg port
item.description:
Nearly 9,278 cargo-laden containers worth several thousand crore taka have remained stranded at Chittagong Port for years, occupying up to one-fifth of its storage capacity and worsening congestion despite repeated efforts to auction them.
According to officials at the Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) and Chittagong Custom House, 9,278 containers carrying around 200,000 tonnes of imported goods are awaiting auction at the port's terminals and container yards.
Many of the containers have remained at the port for 10 to 15 years, with much of the cargo damaged or no longer usable.
Under port regulations, imported goods left unclaimed for 30 days after being unloaded from a vessel must be auctioned or destroyed through customs. However, procedural delays and other complications have allowed thousands of containers to remain at the port for years.
Officials said the abandoned containers now occupy 15% to 20% of the port's operational space, reducing its capacity to handle fresh import and export cargo.
Importers abandoned the consignments for various reasons, including falling market prices, incomplete documentation, customs disputes and other regulatory complications.
Although thousands of containers are awaiting disposal, Chittagong Custom House auctions only 20 to 30 containers each month through open bidding. Perishable goods such as oranges, mandarins, dates and ginger are usually sold through these auctions, while some consignments are disposed of through e-auctions.
Port data show the backlog includes 2,700 twenty-foot containers and 6,578 forty-foot containers.
Commodore Amin Ahmed Abdullah, member (Marine and Harbour) of the Chittagong Port Authority, said removing the auction-eligible containers would significantly improve port operations.
"These containers occupy around 15% to 20% of the port's capacity. Clearing them would free up a substantial area for handling new import and export cargo," he said.
Custom House officials said 2,697 containers have so far been enlisted for auction, while approval has been granted for 1,619 of them.
Last year, 493 containers were handed over to successful bidders after auction, while another 495 have been cleared so far this year, bringing the total to 988 containers over the past 18 months.
However, several hundred newly abandoned containers have been added to the auction list during the same period, leaving the overall backlog largely unchanged.
Sharif Md Al Amin, assistant commissioner at Chittagong Custom House, said the auction process must follow legal procedures.
"There is a prescribed process for auctioning goods stored in containers. Procedural requirements have caused delays, but the auction process is continuing and efforts are being made to speed it up," he said.
Khairul Alam Sujan, former director of the Bangladesh Shipping Agents' Association and former vice-president of the Bangladesh Freight Forwarders Association, said prolonged delays have caused significant losses.
"Goods have deteriorated after remaining inside containers for years, while many containers have also become unusable. Shipping agents are suffering losses. We have repeatedly urged the authorities to expedite the auction process through letters and industry meetings," he said.
Industry stakeholders said resolving the longstanding backlog is essential to easing congestion at Bangladesh's busiest seaport and improving the efficiency of the country's import-export trade.

item.title: Fuel shortage rumors cause rush at petrol pumps in Rajshahi
item.description:
Rumors of a sudden fuel shortage in Rajshahi have triggered large crowds at several filling stations across the city and surrounding rural areas, with motorcycle riders and other vehicle owners rushing to refuel. However, petrol pump owners have confirmed that there is no actual shortage of fuel and that the rush was caused by misinformation circulating on social media.
The rumors began spreading on social media platforms after Tuesday evening, prompting many people to visit filling stations to top up their tanks in anticipation of a possible shortage. As a result, several petrol pumps in Rajshahi city and the district witnessed unusually long queues.
A visit to different filling stations found long lines of motorcycles, private cars, and other vehicles waiting for fuel. The situation was reportedly more crowded at some pumps in rural areas than in the city. Heavy crowds were seen at GM, Lata, Sarkar, Chhanda, and Alam filling stations in areas including Nowdapara and Shalbagan.
At Habib Filling Station, petrol and octane supplies ran out, leaving only diesel available for sale. Meanwhile, more than a hundred motorcycles and vehicles were seen waiting in line at Ruchita Filling Station.
A motorcycle rider, Sohel Rana, said, “I heard that a fuel shortage could occur again like before, so I came to fill my tank in advance.”
Another rider, Zakaria, said, “I saw reports about a possible fuel shortage on Facebook after evening and immediately came to get fuel. But when I arrived, I found a very long queue. I am still waiting and have not received fuel yet.”
Filling station officials said fuel supplies remain normal and that the temporary pressure at some stations was caused by the sudden increase in customers. They emphasized that the situation was not due to any actual shortage.
Rajshahi Petrol Pump Owners’ Association President Momimul Haque said, “There is no fuel shortage. People are buying more fuel than they normally need because of rumors, which is creating unnecessary pressure. We urge everyone not to believe rumors and to purchase fuel according to their requirements. Creating panic may lead to an artificial crisis.”
Meanwhile, the verified Facebook page of the Rajshahi District Administration issued a public notice stating that the district has adequate fuel reserves and that supply operations are running normally.
The notice urged people not to purchase or store excessive amounts of fuel based on rumors or misleading information. It requested residents to buy fuel only as needed and cooperate in maintaining a stable supply system.
The district administration also said it is regularly monitoring market conditions in coordination with relevant authorities. Any person or organization found attempting to create an artificial shortage, raise prices unfairly, or disrupt the market through hoarding will face legal action under existing laws.

item.title: Jamuna erosion halts traffic on Tangail–Tarakanndi Road
item.description:
Rising water levels in the Jamuna River and strong currents have triggered severe erosion in the Sakaria area of the Tangail–Tarakanndi regional highway, threatening the river protection embankment, the Bhuyapur–Tarakanndi road, nearby settlements, and business establishments.
Erosion began on a 25-metre section of the highway near the Jamuna River in Sakaria under Gopalpur Upazila on Sunday afternoon. Following the situation, authorities suspended all vehicle movement on the road. The disruption has forced vehicles to take alternative routes, causing significant inconvenience to commuters.
The Tangail Water Development Board (WDB) has started efforts to contain the erosion by placing geobags at the affected site.
Local residents said erosion has been affecting the area for around one and a half months. They claimed that early preventive measures could have helped avoid the current crisis. Residents warned that if the road collapses completely, communication links will be severely disrupted, affecting thousands of families.
As erosion intensified on Sunday afternoon, parts of the roadside began collapsing into the river. Earlier, locals attempted to slow the river current by placing large tree trunks into the water near the affected area as an immediate protective measure.
Local schoolteacher Moyna said effective river management is essential to prevent major changes in the Jamuna’s course in the future. She emphasized that a permanent embankment solution is needed to ensure the safety of both the road infrastructure and riverside communities.
Meanwhile, Water Development Board Executive Engineer Main Uddin said work to place geobags to control the erosion is ongoing.

item.title: Sreepur residents build drain to end two-decade waterlogging woes
item.description:
Residents of Sreepur upazila in Gazipur have taken an inspiring initiative to solve a long-standing waterlogging problem by constructing a drainage system using their own funds, without waiting for government assistance.
A 1,000-foot-long drain is currently being built from Hanu Market in the Nayanpur area to the house of Asaduzzaman, extending towards Deco Garments. The project, funded and managed by local residents, has drawn appreciation for addressing a public problem through collective community action.
For nearly two decades, people living and working in the area have suffered from severe waterlogging on the Maona-Dhanua regional road, especially during the rainy season. The stagnant water has caused major difficulties for students, garment workers, commuters, drivers, and local business owners. Regular movement became challenging as roads remained submerged for months, creating health risks and disrupting economic activities.
Frustrated by years of waiting for a permanent solution, around 40 families from the area joined together to construct the drain with their own money. Residents involved in coordinating the project said their main goal is to establish an effective drainage system and permanently reduce the suffering caused by water accumulation.
They believe the new drain will help decrease mosquito breeding, unpleasant odours, and the spread of waterborne diseases. They also hope the initiative will encourage other communities to work together to solve local problems instead of depending only on government support.
Businessman Rafiqul Mia said the waterlogging had created serious problems for everyone who used the road.
“Students of nearby schools and colleges, garment workers, passengers, drivers, and local residents all suffered because of the stagnant water. During the rainy season, travelling through the area became extremely difficult. The new drain will help remove the water quickly and make the road more convenient for everyone,” he said.
Auto-rickshaw driver Foyez Uddin said rapid industrial growth in the area had reduced natural drainage channels, causing rainwater to remain trapped on the road.
“Due to the absence of a proper drainage system, people had to walk through dirty water and vehicles faced difficulties moving for years. As road improvement work is currently underway, residents decided that this was the right time to construct the drain,” he said.
He added that the community took the initiative because people could no longer tolerate the recurring problem and wanted a practical solution.
Students Rakibul Islam, Sujon, Morzina, and Alpana Akter said the road remained underwater for four to five months every year.
“During the rainy season, crossing the area became almost impossible. Rickshaws and bicycles often could not pass through the water. Many students had to return home after falling into muddy water and getting their clothes dirty,” they said.
Fruit trader Abdul Razzaq described the initiative as a positive example of cooperation among local people.
“Residents have come forward to solve a public problem using their own resources. This shows how collective efforts can create meaningful change,” he said.
Grocery shop owner Ismail Hossain said the temporary inconvenience caused by the construction work was acceptable because the project would provide long-term benefits.
“We have suffered from waterlogging for many years. Once the drain is completed, residents and businesses will benefit greatly,” he said.
Local BNP leader and Maona Union Parishad chairman candidate Ariful Islam Sarker praised the residents’ efforts, saying ongoing road development work provided a suitable opportunity to build the drainage system.
Sreepur Upazila Engineer of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), Touhid Ahmed, said proper drainage was essential to address long-term waterlogging problems.
“However, if the relevant authorities had been informed before starting the work, the process could have been more organised. Residents have been advised to submit an application, and the matter will be reviewed according to official procedures,” he said.

The forest that makes its own rain
item.description:
When people imagine where rain begins, they usually picture dark clouds gathering over the ocean before drifting across continents.
But in the Amazon rainforest, one of Earth’s greatest rainmakers, the story begins much closer to the ground, inside billions of trees.
Every day, the Amazon releases more than 20 billion tons of water vapour into the atmosphere -- roughly the same amount of water the Amazon River empties into the Atlantic Ocean.
Unlike the river, however, this immense flow is invisible. It rises silently through countless leaves before returning to Earth as rainfall.
For decades, scientists believed forests simply existed because of rain. Research has since revealed a far more remarkable reality: forests also create much of the rain they depend on.
As renowned conservation biologist Thomas E Lovejoy once observed, “Few people are aware that the Amazon makes about half of its own rainfall.”
The process begins with transpiration, a natural cycle in which trees absorb water through their roots and release it into the atmosphere through microscopic pores in their leaves.
As the water vapour rises, it cools, condenses and forms clouds that eventually return as rain.
Trees contribute in another important way.
They release organic compounds that help create aerosols, tiny airborne particles that act as gathering points for water droplets.
These particles make cloud formation more efficient, increasing the likelihood of rainfall.
Home to an estimated 390 billion trees spanning nearly 16,000 species, the Amazon functions as a vast biological water-recycling system.
Rain does not simply fall, flow away and disappear. Instead, trees absorb it, return it to the atmosphere and help generate fresh rainfall as winds carry moisture deeper into the continent.
Scientists describe this remarkable process as moisture recycling.
A 2018 study published in Nature Climate Change found that forests generate “rainfall cascades,” in which moisture released from one region contributes to rainfall hundreds, even thousands, of kilometres away, allowing the cycle to continue across South America.
This recycled moisture travels through the atmosphere in invisible streams known as “flying rivers.”
These airborne rivers supply rainfall across Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, replenishing rivers, sustaining agriculture, powering hydroelectric plants and providing freshwater for millions of people.
In other words, forests do not simply store water -- they move it.
Their importance extends well beyond biodiversity.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), forests regulate rainfall, recharge groundwater, improve water quality, stabilise river systems and reduce the impacts of floods and droughts.
Replacing these natural services with engineered infrastructure, such as irrigation networks and flood-control systems, would cost governments billions of dollars.
Yet this extraordinary water cycle is under growing threat.
Agricultural expansion, cattle ranching, logging and mining continue to remove vast areas of the Amazon.
According to the World Resources Institute, millions of hectares of forest have been lost in recent years, weakening one of the planet’s most important climate-regulating systems.
As forests disappear, less water returns to the atmosphere.
Rainfall declines, droughts become more severe, and a dangerous feedback loop begins: fewer trees produce less rain, while reduced rainfall makes forests increasingly vulnerable to further degradation.
Scientists Thomas Lovejoy and Carlos Nobre have warned that if roughly 20–25% of the Amazon is destroyed, large sections of the rainforest could cross a tipping point, gradually transforming into a much drier, savanna-like landscape.
Such a shift would threaten wildlife, agriculture, freshwater supplies and economies across South America.
The consequences would not stop there.
Bangladesh, one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries, is already experiencing increasingly erratic rainfall, floods and extreme heat.
While the Amazon does not directly determine Bangladesh’s weather, protecting the world’s largest forests helps maintain the stability of the global climate system that influences weather patterns everywhere.
The next time rain begins to fall, it is worth remembering that its journey may have started long before clouds appeared overhead.
It began underground, in roots drawing water from the soil, and in billions of leaves quietly returning that moisture to the sky.
Forests are not simply places where rain falls. They are living engines that help create it.
Protecting them is therefore about far more than saving trees, it is about safeguarding one of Earth’s most vital water systems and the millions of lives sustained by every drop it delivers.

item.title: The music in the air
item.description:
There’s almost always a show happening somewhere in Dhaka.
A Warfaze tribute night fills the Bangladesh China Friendship Exhibition Center. A lineup like “Dacca Underground” packs the National Library Auditorium on a random Friday evening. Independent bands perform in cafés. University campuses host open-air concerts.
Tickets cost a few hundred taka, sometimes a few thousand.
Either way, they sell.
It’s not because people lack access to music. Everyone already has YouTube, Spotify and a phone full of downloaded songs.
Yet people still choose to stand in queues, squeeze into crowded halls and spend an evening listening to songs they could have played at home for free.
Listening to a song through headphones and hearing it performed live are simply two different experiences.
The difference has little to do with sound quality. In fact, a streamed track is often technically cleaner than anything you’ll hear in a packed concert hall.
What a live performance offers instead is presence.
Something is happening right now, in this exact room, and it will never happen in quite the same way again.
A recording is fixed. A live performance is an event -- unrepeatable, a little unpredictable, and that unpredictability is precisely the point.
A singer may miss a note. A guitarist may improvise. A crowd may suddenly take over the chorus.
Anything can happen, and you have to be there to witness it.
Composer Edward Elgar had a name for this feeling long before concert selfies and livestreams existed. He believed music was already in the air, waiting to be discovered, and that a performer’s real task was simply to reach out and take their share of it.
It’s a generous way to think about performance. The musician isn’t creating something from nothing, they’re channeling something that already exists.
For a few hours, a room full of strangers gets to receive it together.
Perhaps that’s the real appeal of live music: it turns something invisible into a shared, physical experience.
Psychology offers its own explanation.
When a crowd claps, sways or sings in unison, the brain releases oxytocin and endorphins—the same chemicals associated with social bonding and pain relief.
Sociologist Émile Durkheim called this collective effervescence: the surge of energy people experience when they participate in a shared ritual.
A concert is, structurally, exactly that.
People arrive as strangers, synchronise their attention for a few hours and leave feeling connected to something larger than themselves. Neuroscientists have found that live performance activates the brain’s reward and social bonding circuits more strongly than recorded music.
That’s because of everything a recording cannot offer: eye contact, physical proximity and the simple awareness that hundreds -- or sometimes thousands -- of people are feeling the same emotion at exactly the same moment.
The experience begins long before the first note.
It starts when the ticket is booked, builds while waiting outside the venue and carries through the entire evening. The anticipation is part of the pleasure, not merely the price of admission.
Musicians have been describing this phenomenon for generations, long before neuroscience attempted to explain it.
Carlos Santana has often spoken of concerts in almost spiritual terms, saying his purpose is to give people a sense of transcendence through music. When an audience cries, laughs and dances together, he considers the night successful.
Jon Batiste describes a live performance as a collaboration with the audience, where musicians respond to the crowd’s energy instead of simply broadcasting to it.
Centuries earlier, Beethoven called music “a higher revelation than all wisdom and philosophy,” suggesting it reaches places words cannot.
Even Kurt Cobain, from a very different musical world, saw live performance as one of the most primal releases of human energy -- a physical, almost instinctive experience shared by an entire crowd.
Strip away the poetry, and all of them are describing the same phenomenon scientists observe today: bodies synchronising, emotions aligning and people feeling something together that none of them could experience alone.
Seen that way, the resurgence of live music is hardly surprising.
Streaming never killed our appetite for concerts. If anything, it expanded it by introducing listeners to more artists than ever before.
What it could never replicate was the missing ingredient: the risk of live performance, the chemistry of the crowd and the knowledge that this particular version of the song will never exist again.
Elgar may have been more right than he realised.
The music is already in the air.
A live concert is simply one of the rare moments when hundreds of strangers reach up, and catch it together.

Fakhrul: Local polls likely by year-end or early 2027
item.description:
Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Wednesday said local government elections are likely to be held either by the end of this year or in early 2027, assuring that the polls will be conducted in a free, fair and impartial manner without any political interference.
Speaking as the chief guest at a discussion organized by the Bangladesh Union Parishad Chairmen and Members Association at the auditorium of the Institution of Diploma Engineers, Bangladesh, he said there will be no scope for anyone to influence the elections and that candidates will have to secure victory through the people's support.
Addressing UP chairmen and members, Fakhrul, also BNP secretary general, said elected representatives regularly participate in the festivals of people from different faiths and stressed that communal harmony must be preserved.
Referring to the upcoming local government elections, he said no political party – BNP or Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami – will receive any special privilege. "Chairmen, members and women members will have to be elected through the people's support. This is the true foundation of democracy," he said.
The minister also stressed the need for proper distribution of relief so that the rights of the poor are not violated.
He said a country's democracy and state system become truly strong only when its local government system is effective and empowered, noting that empowering grassroots public representatives will help deliver services to people's doorsteps and further strengthen the foundation of democracy.
Fakhrul said local governments in developed countries serve as the foundation of administration, justice, healthcare and various public services.
"But since independence, Bangladesh has not been able to bring its local government system to that desired level of strength. Now is the time to empower local government in the true sense," he said.
The minister described UP chairmen and members as the closest representatives of the people at the grassroots who understand local problems, needs, and opportunities better than anyone else, pledging to discuss their allowances with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to ensure they receive a more respectable level of benefits.
He underscored the need for making local government more effective and stronger to institutionalize development and democracy.
Fakhrul said local representatives should be involved in determining beneficiaries of various government programs, including social safety net initiatives.
He also called for greater empowerment of women and improvements in the country's education system, saying Bangladesh will not be able to move forward without educational advancement.
The minister said healthcare services should also be brought closer to local government institutions so they can play a greater role in improving public health services.

item.title: Trump’s special envoy due in Dhaka to sound out Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction
item.description:
Sergio Gor, the US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia, is set to arrive in Dhaka on 30 July to have a clear understanding of Bangladesh's foreign policy priorities and direction.

Diplomats consider this visit significant in the context of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's Beijing visit, Bangladesh's recent engagements with various countries, and recent regional diplomatic activities.

On the first day of the three-day visit, Sergio Gor will meet with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman.

During his visit, he may also exchange views with political party leaders, professionals, and representatives of civil society.

On the final day, he is scheduled to visit the Rohingya refugee situation in Cox's Bazar firsthand. A high-level government official has confirmed this information.

According to diplomatic sources, the current priorities of Bangladesh's foreign policy, regional strategic positioning, and the future of Dhaka-Washington relations will be the focus of discussions during Sergio Gor's visit.

Particularly after the Prime Minister's visit to China in June, the Foreign Minister's visit to Moscow in the same month, and the visit of Turkey's Foreign Minister to Dhaka, there is growing international interest in Bangladesh's strategic position, and Washington's assessment may be reflected in this visit.

Since the BNP government took office in February, US Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs, Paul Kapoor, visited Bangladesh in March, and in May, Brendan Lynch, Assistant Trade Representative for South and Central Asia, also visited.

When asked, Muhammad Sufiur Rahman, former permanent representative of Bangladesh at the UN mission in Geneva and Senior Research Fellow at North South University's South Asia Institute of Policy and Governance (SIPG), told Prothom Alo that since the new government took office, Sergio Gor is likely to try to get a clear understanding of Bangladesh's engagements with various countries and future foreign policy plans during his visit to Dhaka.

Based on this understanding, the US foreign policy direction regarding Bangladesh might be redefined during President Trump's tenure over the next two years. In such a context, Sergio Gor’s visit to Dhaka holds special significance.

Seeing with one's own and others' eyes

During the current government's tenure, Bangladesh's engagements with countries and coalitions such as China, Russia, Turkey, and the European union have become visible. After the new government took office, there were initial indications of Bangladesh advancing positively with India. However, discomfort remains in the relationship between the two countries.

International relations analysts believe Sergio Gor, through this visit, will want to understand the overall direction of Bangladesh's future diplomacy in bilateral and international relations.

From the US perspective, there may be special emphasis on three issues:

Firstly, the discomfort of the US regarding China is no secret. Thus, he will try to understand how Bangladesh’s relations with China will evolve in the short and long term.

Secondly, the effectiveness of the agreement on reciprocal trade or ART with Bangladesh is important. This agreement stipulates that Bangladesh cannot enter into free trade or preferential economic agreements with countries not fully market-based. If it does, the US can cancel the agreement and reinstate previous mutual tariff rates. Hence, this visit holds economic, political, and strategic significance when considering bilateral relations.

Thirdly, questions may be raised about Bangladesh’s plans for its short and long-term relationship with India. Since government-level communication with India has decreased, the U. S. might want to understand which direction the future of the two neighbours’ relationship is heading through this visit.

Security analyst and President of Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies (BIPSS), Major General (Retd.) ANM Muniruzzaman, told Prothom Alo that Sergio Gor's first visit to Bangladesh as the US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia is significant.

Especially considering the Prime Minister's recent China visit and Bangladesh's links with various countries, he will seek to understand the new government’s foreign policy direction in Bangladesh.

Based on understanding Bangladesh's future plans on the international stage, he has the opportunity to play a role in the scope of relations between the two countries as a special envoy.

Rain also fell in the capital on Wednesday. According to the BMD, 30 millimetres of rainfall was recorded in the capital during the 24-hour period from 6:00 am on Wednesday to 6:00 am today.

In its weather forecast for Dhaka and surrounding areas covering the six-hour period from 7:00 am, the department said the sky would remain cloudy, with rain accompanied by thunderstorms likely.

Beyond the capital, Khulna, Barishal and Chattogram divisions are expected to experience light to moderately heavy rainfall at most places today.

Similar weather conditions are also likely in many areas of Rajshahi, Rangpur, Mymensingh and Sylhet divisions.

Meanwhile, the meteorological department has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall at places in Barishal and Chattogram divisions.

The department also said that daytime temperatures may fall slightly across the country today, while night-time temperatures are expected to remain largely unchanged.

In its forecast for the country's inland river ports, valid from 9:00 am to 6:00 pm today, the BMD said that Khulna, Barishal, Patuakhali, Noakhali, Cumilla, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar and Sylhet may experience rain accompanied by squally winds of 45–60 km/h. Inland river ports in these areas have been advised to display Local Cautionary Signal No. 1.

According to the BMD, the axis of the monsoon trough extends through India’s Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and the southern part of Bangladesh to Assam of India. One of its extensions reaches the north-west Bay of Bengal.

The weather forecast further said that the monsoon remains active over southern Bangladesh, fairly active elsewhere across the country, and moderate over the northern Bay of Bengal.

item.title: Support for protests grows in Delhi
item.description:
The confrontation between the Indian central government and protesting students, along with opposition politicians, intensified further on Wednesday.

Proceedings in both Houses of Parliament were disrupted for the third consecutive day.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, expressing support for every demand raised by the protesting students, said that 154 examination paper leaks had occurred over the past decade, yet not a single perpetrator had been convicted.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said the student community was demanding the removal of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, describing it as a legitimate demand. He said the education minister was corrupt and incompetent.

He also backed the students' demand for an apology from the prime minister and called for those responsible for atrocities against students to be punished.

He said the Congress Party supported every one of the students' demands.

Students remained steadfast in their demand for the education minister's resignation, and the protest site at Jantar Mantar returned to its earlier atmosphere. Thousands of students gathered on Wednesday despite the rain.

At one point, Delhi Police disconnected the electricity supply to Jantar Mantar and prevented food and drinking water from reaching the protest site, causing hardship for the demonstrators. However, as time passed, ordinary citizens stepped forward in support. Thousands of people distributed food free of charge.

People from various professions across the country sent food and drinking water to Jantar Mantar through food delivery services such as Swiggy, Zomato, and Foodpanda.

Congress leader Rahul GandhiThose responsible for atrocities against students to be punished.

Around the protest site, many people set up tea stalls, brought home-cooked meals, or distributed fruit free of charge. By Wednesday, so much food had arrived that protest leaders appealed on social media for people to stop sending additional supplies.

Delhi has rarely witnessed such spontaneous public support for any protest movement. Some observers have compared the movement with youth-led protests in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka.

In support of the movement, demonstrators also staged a protest in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, on Wednesday. According to Indian newspaper The Hindu, police detained more than 100 people during the demonstration outside Gujarat University.

Protests at parliament complex

Opposition parties remained firm in their demand for the removal of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, preventing parliament from debating the examination paper leak issue despite the government's willingness to hold discussions.

As on Monday and Tuesday, proceedings in both Houses remained paralysed throughout Wednesday. Opposition parties had submitted adjournment motions, but the Speaker did not accept them.

In an effort to break the deadlock, two government ministers—Health Minister JP Nadda and Minister in the Prime Minister's Office Jitendra Singh—offered to hold a second round of talks with representatives of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP).

The government announced that CJP representatives had been invited to meet at the health minister's residence at noon on Wednesday. However, student leaders declined the invitation, saying they would not attend talks at ministers' residences.

They insisted that if the government was serious about dialogue, ministers should come to Jantar Mantar. If security was a concern, they said discussions could take place at a neutral venue.

CJP spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka told the media that talks would only be meaningful if the government was prepared to accept the students' demands; otherwise, the meeting would merely waste time.

They noted that one round of discussions had already taken place and that they had submitted a charter of demands, but it had produced no results.

Ashutosh Ranka told the media, "If the government accepts our demands, that will be good. Otherwise, lakhs of people are waiting to come to Delhi. This time we will not stop them. We will not ask them to remain silent."

He added, "We have told the government that what happened on 20 July was merely the 'trailer', not the full film."

Congress leaders staged a sit-in outside the prime minister's residence in New Delhi on Tuesday afternoon to protest against the examination paper leak scandal, demand the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, and condemn alleged police brutality against students.

Union Minister Jitendra Singh visited the protest site and told Rahul Gandhi that the government was willing to hold discussions on the paper leak issue and could begin as early as Wednesday.

However, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders remained firm in their demand for the education minister's removal.

On Wednesday morning, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi, and nearly all opposition leaders arrived at parliament wearing black as a mark of protest.

They demonstrated within the parliament complex and disrupted proceedings in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha while demanding the education minister's resignation.

Former Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said the government was ready for discussions, although the rules governing the debate and its duration would need to be agreed upon.

The opposition dismissed the assurance, prompting both the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the chairman of the Rajya Sabha to adjourn proceedings.

According to government sources, the government remains prepared to hold discussions under any conditions but will not agree to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan under any circumstances, as it considers the demand politically motivated.

However, the students remain unwavering in their demand, and opposition parties continue to support that position.

Meanwhile, several Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders have alleged that foreign forces are behind the protests. Some have suggested that Pakistan, the Khalistan movement, and American billionaire George Soros are involved. They claim that a conspiracy is under way to destabilise Narendra Modi's stable government.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were a matter of serious concern, adding that some people were exploiting young people and students for political gain. He described the situation as worrying.

In an effort to break the deadlock, two government ministers—Health Minister JP Nadda and Minister in the Prime Minister's Office Jitendra Singh—offered to hold a second round of talks with representatives of the Chhatra Janata Party (CJP).

The opposition has rejected those allegations. The Congress leadership had already launched protests in several states in support of the students and has now intensified its campaign.

On Wednesday, Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) leader Sharad Pawar and his daughter Supriya Sule visited the protesters at Jantar Mantar.

“Atrocities have shaken conscience of the entire nation”

On Wednesday, authorities closed 16 Metro stations to prevent people from reaching Jantar Mantar. The closures disrupted daily commuters, and passengers staged protests inside several stations, chanting anti-government slogans. The authorities reopened the stations later that evening.

Against this backdrop, student leaders on Wednesday urged activist Sonam Wangchuk to end his hunger strike.

In a social media post, the CJP wrote, "You have inspired an entire generation. You have motivated us. We request you to end your hunger strike. We will continue our movement until our demands are met."

A delegation of opposition members of parliament also visited Wangchuk in hospital on Wednesday.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday instructed the police to preserve all evidence related to allegations of police brutality, including documents and CCTV footage, and ensure that nothing was destroyed.

Rebuking the police, the judges said, "Students have made allegations of police brutality, yet you claim this is merely part of a publicity campaign? How can that be? These atrocities have shaken the conscience of the entire nation."

item.title: Modi vows punishment for exam fraud fuelling India protests
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS-EDUCATION-DEMONSTRATION

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi vowed on Thursday “stringent punishment” for those involved in exam fraud that has fuelled student anger, in his first direct comments tied to major protests challenging his government.

The comments came after thousands of protesters, ledby the social media-driven Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, rallied in New Delhi on Wednesday, triggering fresh clashes with the police.

“Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth,” he said in a social media post, promising to set up fast-track courts to punish those involved in question paper leaks.

“Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared,” he added.

The protesters, mostly young students, have been demanding the resignation of the education minister over exam paper leaks since last month.

Protests snowballed on Monday after police fired tear gas and baton-charged tens of thousands of demonstrators as they tried to march to parliament on the opening day of the monsoon session.

As tensions escalated, protesters responded by hurling stones, marking the largest street rally in the capital in about five years.

At least 178 people, including security personnel, were injured in the violence, according to the police.

The CJP, which has millions of followers on social media, emerged in May initially as a satirical response to Chief Justice Surya Kant reportedly likening young people to “cockroaches” and “parasites” during a court hearing.

The movement has since broadened its agenda to include concerns over unemployment, opportunities for young people and what it describes as Modi’s increasingly authoritarian style of governance.

The protests have emerged as one of the biggest challenges to Hindu-nationalist Modi since his re-election for a third term in office in 2024.

A series of exam irregularities have undermined trust in India’s testing system, including the leak of a medical entrance question paper that forced more than two million candidates to retake the test.

Another dispute involving the online marking of examinations taken by nearly two million high school students has further fuelled public anger.

President Shahabuddin likely to resign soon
item.description:
• Ill health may be cited as the likely reason for the resignation

  • BNP’s top leadership already conveys a message signalling the resignation

  • The govt and the party are discussing potential successors

  • If the office falls vacant, the Speaker will serve as Acting President

  • Presidential election will be held within 90 days through a vote by MPs

President Mohammed Shahabuddin may resign shortly citing physical illness as the reason, responsible sources have indicated.

According to sources within the government and the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), a message has already been conveyed from the BNP’s high command to President Mohammed Shahabuddin, who was elected during the Awami League administration, requesting him to step down. Simultaneously, high-level discussions are underway regarding his potential successor.

This correspondent spoke on Wednesday night with a source connected to the message delivered to the President from the high-level of the ruling party. Requesting anonymity, the source confirmed that it is highly likely that the President will resign very soon.

Discussions are also taking place within the BNP’s high command regarding the election of the next president. The name of a senior secretary currently serving on a contractual basis in an important government post has suddenly emerged in discussions as a potential successor. Previously, however, the names of senior BNP leaders, including Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain and Abdul Moyeen Khan, were under consideration for the role.

If Mohammed Shahabuddin resigns, the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament) Speaker will temporarily assume the duties of the President in accordance with the Constitution. Subsequently, a new president will be elected by members of parliament within the prescribed timeframe.

As the next general election is scheduled to take place during the tenure of the new president, the question of who becomes the country’s next head of state has gained immense political significance.

Although Mohammed Shahabuddin was elected under the Awami League’s nomination, the BNP did not take steps to replace him immediately upon forming the government.

However, senior BNP leader Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain, whose name was floating in connection with the post, told Prothom Alo that he was unaware of any such development.

When asked about the sudden emergence of a contractually appointed secretary’s name for the presidency, Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain remarked, “I am completely unaware of this matter. Naturally, if such an event occurs (the president’s resignation), many names will be discussed for the vacant office.”

President Shahabuddin feeling 'humiliated', wants to resign after February election

As of yesterday, Wednesday, no official statement or announcement regarding President Mohammed Shahabuddin’s resignation had been issued by Bangabhaban or the government.

However, a source from the Bangabhaban indicated that the President himself has hinted to his subordinate staff to prepare to leave Bangabhaban soon. According to that source, he plans to rest for a period following his resignation and may travel abroad for medical treatment.

What the Constitution says regarding presidential resignation

According to Article 50(3) of the Constitution, the president may resign from office by writing under his hand addressed to the speaker. Furthermore, Article 54 states that if the office of president becomes vacant, or if the president is unable to discharge the functions of his office due to absence, illness, or any other cause, the speaker shall discharge those functions until a new president is elected.

Under Article 123 of the Constitution, upon a vacancy occurring in the office of president by reason of resignation, death, or removal, an election to fill the vacancy must be held within 90 days. The president is elected by the votes of the MPs. Given that the ruling BNP holds a majority in parliament, the nominee put forward by the party will be elected.

Mohammed Shahabuddin’s appointment to the presidency had sparked widespread discussion and criticism even during the Awami League’s tenure.

Among the names circulating, a secretary currently holding a contractual appointment in a major government position is being widely tipped as the leading candidate. Sources noted that his name has been brought forward in light of his administrative expertise and the confidence reposed in him by the top government leadership. However, party and government decision-makers will hold further discussions before arriving at a final decision.

Ruling party strategists are mindful that the new president will have to manage potential political pressure surrounding the upcoming general election. Therefore, background experience and acceptability across the government, opposition parties, and state institutions are being given significant weight.

Mohammed Shahabuddin was sworn in as the 22nd president of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh on 24 April 2023. He was elected unopposed under the nomination of the Awami League. His five-year term was originally scheduled to conclude in April 2028.

Following the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August 2024 amid a student-led mass uprising, the country’s political landscape shifted dramatically. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and left the country at that time. Subsequently, Mohammed Shahabuddin served as president through several critical phases of political transition, including the dissolution of parliament and the formation of the interim government.

Following the mass uprising, student leaders demanded the removal of President Mohammed Shahabuddin. Various organisations associated with the July Movement staged demonstrations, including besieging Bangabhaban, to demand his resignation. However, the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus took no initiatives to remove him.

Later, the BNP returned to power through a general election, resulting in a divergence between the political background of the president and that of the government.

Although Mohammed Shahabuddin was elected under the Awami League’s nomination, the BNP did not take steps to replace him immediately upon forming the government. While speculations regarding the president’s future persisted in political circles following the change of power, neither the government nor the BNP publicly demanded his resignation.

While serving at Islami Bank, Mohammed Shahabuddin was appointed president by the now-ousted Awami League government. Resigning from the bank, he assumed office as president on 24 April 2023.

Mohammed Shahabuddin’s appointment to the presidency had sparked widespread discussion and criticism even during the Awami League’s tenure.

He served as a commissioner of the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) from 2011 to 2016, during which several allegations were raised against him. Later, his close ties with the controversial business conglomerate S. Alam Group became public.

Following his tenure at the ACC, he served as the vice-chairman of the Board of Directors of Islami Bank and as an advisor to NRB Global Bank. Both banks were owned at the time by S. Alam Group, an influential business entity during the Awami League regime, and were subject to extensive financial plundering during that period.

While serving at Islami Bank, Mohammed Shahabuddin was appointed president by the now-ousted Awami League government. Resigning from the bank, he assumed office as president on 24 April 2023.

It was widely discussed within the Awami League that the decision to appoint Shahabuddin was made jointly by the then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her sister Sheikh Rehana. At the time, critics on social media and in various circles referred to the president as a representative of S. Alam.

Sources indicate that the ruling party allowed time to observe whether the president would step down voluntarily. Recently, the sentiments of the BNP high command were communicated to him.

Should the president ultimately resign, it will mark another major structural transition at the highest constitutional level of the state following the mass uprising and the subsequent general election.

Furthermore, it will afford the BNP its first opportunity since coming to power to install a candidate of its own choosing in the presidency.

As the next national parliamentary election is set to take place during the new president’s term, keen interest remains across the political spectrum as to who will assume the office.

item.title: Drivers, commuters suffer as potholes plague Barami-Singhasree road
item.description:
Drivers and commuters are facing severe hardship due to numerous potholes and craters along a 2km stretch of the Barami-Singhasree road in Gazipur's Sreepur upazila.
The bitumen surface has peeled off, exposing bricks and sub-base materials. During rainfall, water accumulates in the potholes, making the road muddy and hazardous for both vehicles and pedestrians.
Heavy and light vehicles are forced to move slowly, causing traffic congestion and damaging vehicle suspensions and other mechanical parts. Drivers say visibility at night makes the situation even more dangerous, with potholes often leading to minor and major accidents.
The damaged section stretches from Barami in Sreepur to the Singhasree Bridge over the Shitalakshya River.
As the bridge is toll-free, the road has become a popular route for long-distance heavy vehicles, accelerating its deterioration.
Thousands of commuters from Pakundia in Kishoreganj, Monohardi in Narsingdi, and Kapasia and Sreepur in Gazipur use the road daily to travel to Gazipur and Dhaka. It also serves as a key transport route for residents of Tok, Singhasree, Rayed and Barishab unions in Kapasia.
Passengers and drivers said trucks and freight vehicles travelling from Sylhet, Bhairab and other regions frequently use the road as a bypass because of the toll-free bridge, increasing pressure on the road.
Students of Barami Degree College, Jewel Rana and Maria Akhter, said they fear accidents while travelling by CNG-run autorickshaw because of the damaged road.
Students of Sreepur Government College, Tanjila Akhter and Sumaiya, said they regularly get stuck in traffic jams caused by the potholes and often fail to reach college on time.
Babul Mia, a resident of Singhasree and a garment factory supervisor in Maona, said his daily commute has doubled because he must ride slowly over the damaged road.
CNG driver Kafil Uddin said frequent repairs have become unavoidable as the road damages vehicles almost every week.
"If the road is not repaired soon, vehicles will stop using it altogether," he said.
Autorickshaw driver Abu Musa said the risk of accidents increases during rain when potholes become submerged.
"Passengers are reluctant to travel on this road because of safety concerns," he said.
Local residents Rahim Uddin and Hafizul Islam said the road is an important link for people in Kapasia, Sreepur, Pakundia and Monohardi, but repeated demands for repairs have gone unanswered.
Traders Rafiqul Islam and Nurul Amin said poor road conditions have increased transport costs and delayed the movement of goods, affecting businesses.
They urged the authorities to repair the road without delay and take measures to regulate the movement of heavy vehicles.
Sreepur Upazila Engineer Touhid Ahmed of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) said a proposal has already been submitted to widen and repair the road.
"We hope work will begin after the necessary administrative and procurement processes are completed," he said.

item.title: Taking our ties with the Maldives further
item.description:
The Maldives' growing interest in recruiting more skilled Bangladeshi professionals while broadening bilateral cooperation beyond traditional labour migration is certainly a promising development for both countries.
For decades, Bangladeshi workers have played an indispensable role in supporting the Maldivian economy, particularly in construction and hospitality.
Now, as the island nation expands its healthcare, tourism, and infrastructure sectors, its demand for nurses, accountants, and other skilled professionals presents Bangladesh with a valuable opportunity to elevate the nature of this partnership.
This prospect, however, must be approached strategically if it is to deliver maximum mutual benefit.
Bangladesh cannot simply view this as another overseas employment destination. Rather, it should treat it as an incentive to invest more heavily in technical education, vocational training, professional certification, and language skills.
Producing a workforce that consistently meets international standards will not only strengthen Bangladesh's reputation abroad but also enable workers to command better wages and enjoy improved career prospects.
The opportunities extend well beyond labour exports: Discussions on greater cooperation in trade, tourism, renewable energy, maritime connectivity, and climate diplomacy point to a partnership with significant long-term potential.
A direct shipping route, if realized, could reduce transport costs and facilitate greater commercial exchange, while collaboration on climate resilience is particularly relevant given the shared vulnerabilities of both low-lying nations.
The responsibility now lies with policy-makers in both countries to translate these encouraging discussions into tangible outcomes.
Bangladesh must strengthen skills development, improve worker protection, and ensure ethical recruitment practices, while the Maldives should continue creating transparent pathways for skilled migrants and expanding avenues for broader economic cooperation.
This evolving relationship represents an opportunity to build a mature, diversified partnership that benefits both economies. With careful planning, sustained diplomatic engagement, and a commitment to shared growth, Bangladesh and the Maldives can turn this promising prospect into a lasting success.

item.title: The push for export diversification
item.description:
The government's ambition to achieve double-digit export growth in promising sectors such as leather, agro-processing, and light engineering is an encouraging sign for Bangladesh's economy, but only if it translates into reality.
At a time when the country is preparing for its post-LDC future, broadening the export base is no longer merely desirable -- it is essential.
The Commerce Ministry's emphasis on supporting these sectors and creating a more business-friendly environment reflects an understanding that Bangladesh must reduce its overwhelming dependence on ready-made garments if it is to sustain long-term economic growth.
The garment industry has been the backbone of Bangladesh's export success for decades, but relying too heavily on a single sector has exposed our economy to global market fluctuations, shifting trade policies, and changing consumer demand. Diversification is, therefore, a safeguard against future uncertainty.
Fortunately, Bangladesh possesses considerable untapped potential. Leather and leather goods, pharmaceuticals, agro-processing, information technology, light engineering, shipbuilding, and jute-based products all have the capacity to become significant export earners.
However, unlocking that potential requires sustained investment in infrastructure, uninterrupted energy supplies, simplified regulations, easier access to finance, and stronger support for innovation and research.
Particular attention should also be paid to small and medium-sized enterprises and emerging entrepreneurs. These businesses often struggle to enter international markets due to limited resources and inadequate institutional support.
By facilitating participation in international trade fairs, strengthening export promotion initiatives, and helping businesses comply with global quality standards, the government can nurture the next generation of exporters.
Ultimately, export diversification should be viewed as a national priority rather than a short-term policy objective. A broader export portfolio will strengthen economic resilience, create higher-value employment, and enhance Bangladesh's competitiveness in the global marketplace.
If backed by consistent reforms and effective implementation, the government's vision of export growth can become far more than an aspiration -- it can serve as the foundation for a stronger and more sustainable economy.

item.title: Climate action can save 88,000 lives a year
item.description:
The latest estimate that air pollution contributes to nearly 88,000 premature deaths every year in Dhaka should stop us in our tracks. Behind this staggering number are parents who never return home, children whose lungs never fully develop, older people whose lives are cut short, and families burdened by illness that was largely preventable.
We often discuss air pollution and climate change as two separate crises. In reality, they are two symptoms of the same problem.
The overwhelming majority of greenhouse gases and harmful air pollutants originate from the same sources: Burning fossil fuels in power plants, industries, brick kilns, transport systems, and households.
Every litre of diesel burned, every ton of coal consumed, and every inefficient brick kiln operating releases carbon dioxide that warms the planet alongside fine particulate matter and toxic gases that damage human health.
This means that every climate action is also an air quality intervention.
When we replace fossil fuels with renewable energy, improve public transport, electrify vehicles, increase energy efficiency, modernize industries, or phase out polluting brick kilns, we are not only reducing Bangladesh's contribution to climate change but allowing people to breathe cleaner air almost immediately.
Scientists often describe this as a "co-benefit" of climate action. But perhaps that term understates its significance. Saving tens of thousands of lives every year is not merely an added benefit; it should be one of the primary reasons for accelerating climate action.
Too often, climate mitigation is portrayed as an expensive obligation undertaken for future generations or to meet international commitments under the Paris Agreement. That framing misses the enormous domestic benefits.
Cleaner air means fewer heart attacks and strokes. It means fewer cases of asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, diabetes, and complications during pregnancy. It means healthier children, more productive workers, lower healthcare costs, and stronger economic growth.
In other words, climate policy is public health policy.
Yet our institutions often continue to treat these issues separately.
Air pollution is addressed through environmental regulation and public health measures, while climate change is discussed in the context of international agreements, emissions targets, and energy transitions. Different ministries, different budgets, different strategies, but the same sources of pollution.
This separation risks missing one of the greatest opportunities available to Bangladesh.
Imagine if every transport investment, every industrial policy, every energy project, and every urban development plan were evaluated not only for its contribution to economic growth and carbon reduction, but also for the number of lives it could save through cleaner air.
Climate and clean-air policies should not compete for attention or funding -- they should reinforce one another through a single integrated strategy.
Bangladesh has already demonstrated remarkable leadership in climate adaptation. From cyclone preparedness to community-based resilience, the country has shown that it can pioneer innovative responses to climate risks.
The next chapter of leadership should be to integrate climate mitigation and clean-air policies into one coherent national agenda -- not because international negotiators demand it, but because Bangladeshi citizens deserve clean air.
This shift is becoming increasingly important.
Bangladesh is urbanizing rapidly, electricity demand continues to grow, transport systems are expanding, and industrial production is increasing.
Decisions made today about energy infrastructure, mobility, urban planning, and manufacturing will determine both our emissions trajectory and the quality of the air millions breathe every day.
Fortunately, many of the solutions are already known.
Expanding renewable energy reduces dependence on fossil fuels. Investing in reliable and affordable public transport reduces congestion and vehicle emissions. Accelerating electric mobility, improving industrial efficiency, modernizing brick production, protecting urban green spaces, and enforcing air quality regulations all deliver immediate health gains while contributing to long-term climate goals.
These are not competing priorities. They are mutually reinforcing investments in Bangladesh's future.
International experience consistently shows that the economic value of improved health often offsets a substantial share of the cost of climate mitigation. Fewer hospital admissions, lower medical expenditures, reduced absenteeism, and higher labour productivity generate benefits that are rarely captured in traditional climate debates.
Perhaps it is time to change the conversation.
Instead of asking: "Can Bangladesh afford climate action?" we should ask: "Can Bangladesh afford the human and economic cost of treating climate change and air pollution as separate challenges?"
Every year of delay means thousands of avoidable deaths, millions of sick days, and billions of taka in lost productivity and healthcare costs.
The estimate of 88,000 lives lost annually should become more than another alarming statistic. It should become a catalyst for a new way of governing -- one that recognizes that reducing greenhouse gas emissions and cleaning the air are not parallel ambitions, but two outcomes of the same decisions.
Bangladesh does not have to choose between economic development and climate action. The smartest development pathway is also the healthiest one.
By accelerating the transition towards cleaner energy, cleaner transport, cleaner industries, and more sustainable cities, the country can simultaneously reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve competitiveness, and protect the health of millions.
The air we breathe and the climate we inherit are inseparable. Our policies should be as well.
If Bangladesh succeeds in bringing climate and clean-air policies together under one integrated vision, it will not only help slow global warming. It could save tens of thousands of Bangladeshi lives every year.
That is perhaps the strongest argument for climate action of all.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: Cockroach Janta Party protest: How liberal scepticism induces paralysis in oppositional politics
item.description:
The most corrosive feature of India’s current political landscape is not merely the overweening power of the ruling dispensation, but the fundamental collapse of the capacity to distinguish truth from fiction among those who seek to oppose it.
In a climate where truth is already a precarious commodity, a new and more insidious pathology has taken hold: A habit of suspicion that sees every stirring of civic life not as a sign of democratic vitality, but as a meticulously choreographed puppet show.
The discussions over the past few weeks about the emergence of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party and the hunger strike by Ladakhi activist Sonam Wangchuk provide a clinical study in this self-inflicted paralysis.
Rather than engaging with the substance of these mobilizations, a significant section of liberal opinion-making has retreated into a hall of mirrors.
By framing these movements as “staged” or as “false flag” operations engineered by the state, the Opposition’s intellectual vanguard is committing a double error. It is alienating potential allies and, more tragically, it is undermining the very possibility of political action.
The tragedy of contemporary Indian liberalism is its transition from a project of institutional defence to a project of conspiratorial narcissism. There is a seductive comfort in believing that everything is a ruse. It relieves the commentator of the hard work of organizing and it protects the ego from the messiness of unpredictable political outcomes.
If every protest is a plant, then the failure to mobilize need not be explained.
But this “narrative suspicion” has costs. In any healthy democracy, spontaneous civic dissent is a bridge that provides the raw material political parties must refine into institutional pressure.
When influential voices preemptively dismiss these movements as “engineered,” they do the ruling party’s work for them. They create a vacuum where there should be an alliance. They signal to the public that no one -- not even the ascetic or the aggrieved student -- can be trusted.
This does more than just critique the state: It inadvertently validates the state’s claim that all dissent is manufactured and illegitimate.
Political judgement is being turned into a personal performance for social media platforms. Driven by the incentives of the attention economy, pundits now prioritize the “sharp take” over the patient gathering of evidence.
There is a status-seeking dimension to this scepticism. To be the one who sees through the charade offers a sense of intellectual superiority that a more cautious, evidence-based approach lacks.
Yet, this is a hollow victory. While the commentator gains followers, the political movement loses its footing.
The consequence is a “demobilization.” Opposition parties, already hesitant and strategically adrift, are further spooked by these whispers of sabotage.
They recoil from engagement, fearing they might be the dupes of a grander malign scheme.
This fragmentation of the anti-establishment discourse ensures that civic energy, rather than being channeled into a coherent challenge to power, is dissipated in a series of internecine squabbles over authenticity.
If Opposition politics is to regain any semblance of traction, it must first recover a sense of democratic faith.
This does not mean a naive acceptance of every claim. Scepticism is a vital democratic virtue. But scepticism must be a tool for uncovering truth, not a shield for avoiding the responsibility of political engagement.
Responsible critics must move away from the sensationalist shortcut and toward a more demanding standard of verification.
They must learn to distinguish between the presence of suspicious actors (who exist in every movement) and the underlying legitimacy of the grievance.
To treat every protest as a tactical feint by the regime is to grant the regime a degree of omnipotence it does not possess.
Democracy thrives on the unpredictability of the street and the courage of the individual actor. By drowning these in a sea of conspiracy, the liberal intelligentsia is not protecting the republic -- it is ensuring its own irrelevance.
The task of the critic is not to unmask every movement until nothing remains, but to provide the intellectual architecture that allows genuine dissent to stand.
Without that, the only thing being eaten by conspiracy is the possibility of a democratic future.
