item.title: EC drafts new UP polls code with AI curbs, stricter campaign rules
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) has drafted a new code of conduct for Union Parishad elections, proposing a raft of changes, including restrictions on the use of microphones, a ban on collecting voters' NID cards and mobile phone numbers aiming to influence votes, tighter rules on AI-generated campaign content and higher penalties for electoral misconduct.
The proposed code prohibits the use of microphones and other sound-amplifying devices before 12pm and after sunset in any election area, replacing the existing campaign hours of 2pm to 8pm.
The EC has updated the code following amendments to the Local Government (Union Parishad) Act, 2009, under which Union Parishad elections will be held on a non-partisan basis after the abolition of political party symbols.
Among the major changes are a ban on making transactions through mobile financial service (MFS) and traditional campaign posters, formal recognition of digital and social media campaigning under strict regulations, restrictions on the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI), permission for campaign caravans and a proposal to raise the maximum fine for violating the code from Tk10,000 to Tk50,000.
Under the draft, loudspeaker volume during campaigns must not exceed 60 decibels, while only one microphone will be permitted at a time for campaign activities or street meetings within a ward.
The proposed code also prohibits candidates or their supporters from collecting voters' or their family members' NID numbers to influence voting or gathering mobile phone numbers for conducting transactions through MFS, such as bKash, Nagad, Rocket or Upay.
In a significant change, the EC has formally allowed election campaigns through digital and social media, subject to a series of restrictions.
Candidates, election agents and campaigners will have to submit the names of their social media platforms, account IDs, email addresses and other identifying information to the returning officer before launching online campaigns.
The draft bars the malicious use of AI in election campaigns and prohibits the creation or dissemination of harmful content, including hate speech, misinformation, manipulated images, and fabricated election-related information.
It also bans the use of religion, ethnicity, caste, gender or community-based hate speech, provocative language or the misuse of religious or ethnic sentiments for electoral gains.
The proposed code prohibits the creation, publication, dissemination or sharing of AI-generated or AI-edited false, misleading, biased, hate, obscene, vulgar or defamatory content on social media or any other media with a view to misleading voters or tarnishing the reputation of any candidate or person.
The draft code also slaps a ban on traditional campaign posters while permitting the use of billboards under strict conditions.
Each candidate will be allowed to display only one billboard per ward, with a maximum size of 16 feet by 9 feet, provided it does not obstruct traffic, endanger public safety or harm the environment.
Campaign materials such as banners, leaflets and festoons must be biodegradable and cannot be made of rexine, polythene, plastic or other environmentally harmful materials. PVC banners and plastic coverings will also be prohibited.
To make electioneering more festive, the draft code allows caravan or mobile campaign processions using digital technology or biodegradable materials on vehicles from 12pm until sunset, provided they do not disrupt traffic or cause public inconvenience.
Election campaigning inside educational institutions will remain prohibited, although playgrounds may be used with permission from the authorities as long as academic activities are not disrupted.
The draft also bars city corporation administrators from participating in election campaigns.
The EC has also proposed increasing the penalty for violating the election code. Anyone found guilty of breaching the code may face up to six months' imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk50,000, or both. The existing maximum fine is Tk10,000.
A new provision has been incorporated in the draft code empowering the EC to cancel candidature following an investigation for the violation of the electoral code.

item.title: Ebadot to miss Australia tour as Bangladesh wait on injuries
item.description:
Bangladesh will be forced to tackle ICC World Test Championship pacesetter Australia next month without key fast bowler Ebadot Hossain.
The Asian side are scheduled to take on Australia in a two-match Test series that commences in Darwin on August 13 as part of the ongoing World Test Championship and Ebadot will instead stay in Bangladesh as he gets ready to welcome his first child.
The news on Ebadot has been offset with confirmation that pace spearhead Taskin Ahmed has withdrawn from the Lankan Premier League (LPL) to instead prepare for the Australia tour, where Bangladesh will attempt to improve on their current fourth-place on the World Test Championship standings.
Taskin had been scheduled to feature for the Jaffna Kings at the LPL, but the 31-year-old has decided to do everything he can to prepare for the Australia tour.
“Yeah it is mainly for preparation (for the Australia tour)," Taskin told The Daily Sun.
"We played six back-to-back matches in Zimbabwe, maybe I would have got four matches there (in LPL), after my stint there if I return home and immediately go to Australia my Test match preparation would be hampered, despite a little loss I thought it’s OK.
"The Australia series won’t come around often, that’s why I took the decision, even after having the NOC, so I pulled out from the LPL."
Just whether star pacer Nahid Rana will be fit for the opening Test against Australia remains to be seen, with Bangladesh still awaiting results of scans the star pacer recently had done on his side injury.
The team are also hopeful experienced batter Litton Das will be able to shake off his calf complaint to feature against Australia, with Bangladesh set to arrive Down Under at the start of next month ahead of a three-day warm-up fixture in Darwin against a Cricket Australia XI from August 3.
That contest will provide Bangladesh with some valuable practice ahead of the first Test at the same venue and batting coach Mohammad Ashraful is hoping he will have a full complement of players to choose from.
"It will be tough in Australia, but the positive is that we will travel there early...10–12 days in advance," Ashraful said.
"We will have the opportunity to play a three-day practice match, and hopefully, if all our players are fit, we will be able to perform well there."
While Bangladesh's pace attack has won much of the plaudits for the side's excellent recent form, Ashraful has been happy with the efforts of his batting group despite a slip up in their most recent Test outing against Zimbabwe in Harare when they were dismissed for just 140 and 185 in a massive defeat.
Ashraful is confident his batters will be able to turn that around in Australia despite the strong squad the Aussies recently name, pointing to their good efforts against Pakistan in May when they registered an impressive 2-0 series sweep.
"Our batters did really well over the last seven months. One series can go wrong; one Test match went bad, but in the four Tests prior to that, our batters played extremely well," he said.
"See, we can lose one or two games in different conditions. After playing so well over the last seven months, there is no reason to be demoralised after losing one or two matches, I believe. Obviously, they have gained experience from playing in different conditions."
Series schedule:
First Test: August 13-17, Darwin
Second Test: August 22-26, Mackay

item.title: How Asia fared at World Cup and what comes next
item.description:
A record nine Asian nations took part in the FIFA World Cup 2026, and while there were some high points along the way it was ultimately an underwhelming tournament for the AFC representatives.
Australia and Japan made it to the Round of 32, where each suffered agonisingly close defeats, but five other sides — Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Uzbekistan — finished winless and bottom of their groups, while IR Iran and Korea Republic narrowly failed to progress among the best third-place finishers.
FIFA looks back on the positives and negatives for each side, highlights players who could be set to play key roles in four years' time, and considers what comes next as teams aim to regroup after a chastening experience.
Japan
Hajime Moriyasu and his players headed to North America declaring the aim was to return with the trophy, but while a dramatic comeback against the Netherlands and a biggest-ever World Cup win against Tunisia served as highlights, a meek defeat after taking the lead against Brazil in the Round of 32 saw them eliminated at the first knockout stage for the third consecutive tournament.
Local media reports suggest the coach is set to sign a contract extension until the conclusion of the next Asian Cup, after which his replacement will be charged with continuing the team’s evolution. The likes of Takehiro Tomiyasu, Takefusa Kubo and Ayase Ueda could still all be options for 2030, but the wealth of young talent being produced in Japan will also need to be harnessed to steer them to greater heights.
IR Iran
Having faced numerous obstacles in both qualification and then at the World Cup itself, Iran came as close as you can to securing a Round of 32 berth without quite doing so — finishing ninth in the rankings of third-placed nations when only the top eight progressed.
Along with Spain, Iran were the only nation not to lose a match at the tournament, after they drew 2-2 with New Zealand, 0-0 with Belgium and then 1-1 in a late thriller with Egypt.
The Iran Football Federation has confirmed that head coach Amir Ghalenoei will remain in place through at least the upcoming Asian Cup, with the 61-year-old telling local media that a ‘transition’ around lowering the age profile of the team will begin shortly.
Saudi Arabia
On the face of it, exiting the World Cup with your only defeat coming at the hands of dominant champions Spain is nothing to be ashamed of. However, after their historic win over Argentina in 2022 the Green Falcons will have plenty of regrets having drawn their other two games against Uruguay and the tournament's surprise package Cabo Verde.
It was ultimately a lack of attacking quality that held Georgios Donis' side back, with their only goal coming after Abdulelah Al Amri stabbed in a rebound in the opening draw with Uruguay. For the time being it looks as though the Greek coach will remain in charge for the upcoming Asian Cup, but, as with several of the other AFC sides something of a rebuild will be required, centred upon players such as midfield starlet Musab Al Juwayr.
Australia
One of just two AFC nations to advance from the group stage, the Socceroos did so for a second consecutive tournament. The positives were a robust defensive showing, where they conceded just three goals in four matches, as well as the emergence of some impressive young talent. 22-year-old goalkeeper Patrick Beach, 18-year-old Lucas Herrington, 21-year-old midfielder Paul Okon-Engstler and 20-year-old forward Nestory Irankunda could be long-term options to build the team around.
Conversely, setting aside an own goal in the nation’s extra-time loss to Egypt in the Round of 32, they only managed to score twice in four outings. Finding a consistent No9 remains an issue as Australia, still under the guidance of Tony Popovic, head to the upcoming Asian Cup aiming for a second continental title.
Iraq
Iraq may have exited at the group stage at their first World Cup in 40 years, but they impressed at points in what was arguably the toughest of all groups. Having started brightly against Norway, they fell apart after the break, and went on to suffer further defeats against France and Senegal.
Head coach Graham Arnold is currently in discussions about extending his contract with the IFA and, having put nine of the 12 goals the team conceded down to ‘individual errors’, he can see plenty of positives to take going forward.
Veteran forward Aymen Hussein scored just the second goal at the global finals for the Lions of Mesopotamia in their opener with Norway, but with a core group of players in their mid-20s, the signs are positive that Iraq can show even more four years down the line.
Jordan
Jordan exited their debut World Cup bottom of Group J after three straight defeats, but they were competitive in those losses to Austria, Algeria and then finalists Argentina. Indeed, they managed to score in all three outings, with Ali Olwan grabbing the nation’s first World Cup goal in the 3-1 opening defeat against Austria.
Following the Nashama’s exit, it was announced that head coach Jamal Sellami would be departing his post, with Badou Zaki appointed the day before the World Cup final.
The former goalkeeper captained Morocco at the 1986 FIFA World Cup, where his nation fell 1-0 to West Germany in the Round of 16. His initial challenge will come at the forthcoming Asian Cup, where Jordan are looking to build on a runners-up finish from 2024.

Following that disappointment Hong has departed, and with star Son Heungmin now 34 it looks like Korea will be requiring something of a rebuild — with the onus on core talents like Lee Kangin to come to the fore as the nation targets success at the upcoming Asian Cup and a better showing on the global stage in 2030.
Qatar
Having become the first host nation to fail to make it through the group stage in 2022, reigning Asian champions Qatar were desperate to put in a better showing in North America, and while they were unable to seal a spot in the Round of 32 they did at least claim their first World Cup point after snatching a dramatic injury-time equaliser in their opening game against Switzerland.
Defeats to co-hosts Canada and then Bosnia and Herzegovina prevented Julen Lopetegui’s side from progressing from Group B, but they have the perfect opportunity to bounce back from that disappointment in January when they aim to become continental champions for the third time in a row.
Uzbekistan
The World Cup debutants were eliminated at the group stage after three consecutive defeats, but while results were disappointing there were some positives for the White Wolves. Abbosbek Fayzullaev etched his name into Uzbekistan football history by scoring their first-ever World Cup goal in the 3-1 loss to Colombia, for instance, while Eldor Shomurodov’s sublime effort against Congo DR was voted as the group-stage entry for the Hyundai Goal of the Tournament.
Fabio Cannavaro’s side stayed true to their technical, hard-working approach throughout, and while that ultimately contributed to them tiring a little as games wore on, the likes of 18-year-old Bekhruz Karimov now know what it takes to compete at the global level and will be desperate to build upon these first steps in four years’ time.

item.title: Argentine Football Association says US did not detain its president
item.description:
Argentina's top football officials on Wednesday firmly denied reports that their federation's president and treasurer were detained and questioned upon leaving the United States after the World Cup final.
The Argentine Football Association (AFA) did, however, acknowledge a US investigation into a third party with links to the association.
The organization issued a statement following media reports that its president Claudio Tapia and treasurer Pablo Toviggino had been detained at New York's John F. Kennedy airport before boarding the flight transporting the national squad home after their loss to Spain Sunday.
The pair were reportedly detained for questioning and had their electronic devices seized by US authorities, before being summoned to appear in court regarding AFA's international contracts.
But an AFA statement denied all of the reported claims as "absolutely false."
"All lies," a source from the association told AFP, while the FBI declined to comment.
A district court in Florida had issued a summons targeting "a third party," AFA conceded.
The individual "is being asked to appear before a grand jury and present any documents and communications that may be related to various individuals, including officials" of the federation, it said.
AFA, headed by football heavyweight Tapia since 2017, is the subject of several investigations in Argentina.
One probe is focusing on alleged money laundering, while another relates to tax evasion.
Under former trade unionist Tapia's leadership, AFA's relations with far-right President Javier Milei's administration have grown strained.
Tapia, for instance, strongly opposes the ultra-liberal leader's desire to privatize football clubs across the country.

item.title: Messi-less Miami beat Fire 3-2 to spoil Lewandowski's MLS debut
item.description:
Luis Suarez scored twice and Preston Plambeck grabbed a late winner as Inter Miami, without Lionel Messi, beat Chicago Fire 3-2 on Wednesday to spoil Robert Lewandowski's Major League Soccer debut.
Uruguayan veteran Suarez captained Miami with Messi and fellow Argentine Rodrigo de Paul missing four days after Argentina lost 1-0 to Spain in the World Cup final.
The 37-year-old Poland striker Lewandowski was making his MLS debut having signed from Barcelona after they were crowned Spanish champions.
Prolific goalscorer Lewandowski, who also starred for Bayern Munich from 2014-2022 and has more than 700 goals for club and country, started for Chicago and played 63 minutes.
But it was 20-year-old Plambeck, a product of Miami's youth system, who emerged as the unlikely hero, coming off the bench to score the 87th-minute winner.
Lewandowski had an attempt blocked in the 14th minute, but the Fire got on the board four minutes later through a calamitous own goal.
Miami goalkeeper Rocco Rios Novo, starting in place of Canada World Cup keeper Dayne St. Clair, took a swing at a routine pass back from Ian Fray only to miss and see it roll into the net.
Suarez levelled from the penalty spot in the 27th minute and put Miami ahead in the 51st, firing home after being set-up by a brilliant backheel from German Berterame.
Chicago's South African Puso Dithejane made it 2-2 in the 67th minute only for Plambeck to have the final say by volleying home the rebound for his first Miami goal after goalkeeper Chris Brady had parried Suarez's close-range shot.
